title: flag.ExitOnError bypasses error handling in CLI flag parsing
description:
At internal/cli/app.go:79, the FlagSet uses flag.ExitOnError:

    fs := flag.NewFlagSet("infomunge", flag.ExitOnError)

This causes os.Exit(2) on flag parsing errors, bypassing the normal error handling flow in main(). This makes it impossible to test flag parsing error paths and prevents graceful error reporting.

Fix: change to flag.ContinueOnError and handle the error from fs.Parse() explicitly:

    fs := flag.NewFlagSet("infomunge", flag.ContinueOnError)
    if err := fs.Parse(args); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

title: Separate declaration parsing from declaration evaluation
description:
Problem:
Header and module declaration parsing currently parses syntax and evaluates declarations in the runner. Variable parsing calls the preprocessor and evaluator immediately; function parsing parses Go AST bodies; type/property parsing returns evaluator types; module parsing updates both a typed namespace and raw eval context.

Why it matters:
This couples header syntax, module loading, preprocessing, evaluator internals, and scope mutation. It makes it hard to validate declarations independently, reuse parsing in tooling, or reason about import cycles and declaration ordering without executing expressions.

Evidence:
- `internal/runner/declarations.go` imports evaluator, preprocessor, sourcemap, and go/parser.
- `parseVarDeclFromLinesWithGoContext` preprocesses and evaluates variable expressions.
- `buildFunLambda` preprocesses and parses the function body AST directly.
- `internal/runner/module_parser.go` mutates `rawNs` while constructing `Namespace` entries.

Suggested direction:
Introduce a declaration AST/IR for headers and modules. Parsing should produce version/output/input/import/var/fun/type declarations with source spans. A later binder/evaluator phase should resolve imports and evaluate declarations into a scope.

Acceptance:
- Header/module declaration parsing can be unit-tested without evaluator side effects.
- Module and script headers share the same declaration IR.
- Existing import/var/fun/type behavior remains covered by runner/module cucumber or Go tests.

title: Replace preprocessor mapping invariant panic with recoverable error path
description:
The preprocessor rewriter uses a hard panic in invariant checking, which can terminate the process if any internal mapping drift occurs.

Evidence:
- `internal/preprocessor/preprocessor.go:111`
  - `panic(fmt.Sprintf("mapping invariant violated ..."))`

Why this is significant:
- Even if this is intended as a programming-error detector, panics at this layer can take down CLI/server requests instead of surfacing an actionable parse/runtime error.
- A single malformed internal state should not crash the entire process in production paths.

Proposed fix:
- Replace the panic path with structured error propagation (or guard with recover in the top-level preprocessing/evaluation boundary).
- Preserve invariant details in error context for debugging.
- Add a regression test that validates invariant failures are reported as errors, not panics.

title: unique() conflates different types with same string representation
description:
The `unique()` function in `internal/evaluator/builtins_collection.go:82-96` uses `fmt.Sprintf("%v", item)` as a deduplication key. This causes false collisions between values of different types that have the same string representation:

- `unique([1, "1"])` would drop `"1"` because both int `1` and string `"1"` format to `"1"` via `%v`
- `unique([true, "true"])` would similarly collide
- `unique([nil, "<nil>"])` would collide

Meanwhile, `distinct()` at line 100-126 correctly uses `fmt.Sprintf("%T:%v", item, item)` which includes the type, preventing these collisions.

Either `unique` should include type info like `distinct` does, or the semantic difference between `unique` and `distinct` should be explicitly documented and tested with cross-type scenarios.

Files:
- `internal/evaluator/builtins_collection.go:82-96` (unique — type-agnostic)
- `internal/evaluator/builtins_collection.go:100-126` (distinct — type-aware)

title: Fix CoerceEquals panic on array/object ~= comparisons
description:
`CoerceEquals` can panic when either operand is an uncomparable Go type (`[]interface{}` / `map[string]interface{}`), because it does a direct `left == right` before guarding comparability.

Evidence:
- `internal/evaluator/evaluator.go:624` (`if left == right { ... }`)
- Deterministic failing test repro:
  `go test ./internal/testing/exprgen -run TestExpr_Depth3_DoesNotPanic -rapid.failfile=testdata/rapid/TestExpr_Depth3_DoesNotPanic/TestExpr_Depth3_DoesNotPanic-20260214155635-69581.fail -count=1`
- Failing generated expression: `[] ~= []`

Impact:
- User expressions using `~=` with arrays/objects can crash evaluation instead of returning a value/error.
- This violates no-panic expectations in property tests and is a runtime reliability bug.

Proposed fix:
- Rework `CoerceEquals` to avoid direct interface equality on potentially uncomparable values.
- Reuse `numericEquals`-style comparability checks / `reflect.DeepEqual` for slices/maps before fallback coercion.
- Add focused evaluator tests for `~=` over arrays and objects, including mixed-type coercion cases.

title: Decompose structured XLSX support into workbook, worksheet, and cell layers
description:
`pkg/formats/excel_structured.go` bundles workbook metadata parsing, shared-string decoding, worksheet decoding, row/header validation, worksheet encoding, cell serialization, archive assembly, and XML helpers in one large file.

Evidence:
- `pkg/formats/excel_structured.go:164-241` coordinates structured workbook decode/encode and high-level validation.
- `pkg/formats/excel_structured.go:261-339` parses workbook metadata and shared strings.
- `pkg/formats/excel_structured.go:342-621` mixes worksheet row decoding, cell coercion, header extraction, row validation, worksheet encoding, and per-cell XML rendering.
- `pkg/formats/excel_structured.go:632-780` assembles ZIP/XML output and low-level cell reference helpers.

Why this matters:
- Reader and writer concerns are tightly coupled, so changing one side requires reviewing the entire file.
- The workbook/worksheet/cell concepts do not have clear boundaries, which makes it harder to add features like formulas, styles, or alternative sheet-selection behavior safely.
- A single file now contains both business rules (header semantics, strictness) and transport details (ZIP layout, XML fragments).

Suggested direction:
- Split workbook/package concerns from worksheet row decoding/encoding and from cell coercion/rendering.
- Extract a small model for workbook metadata and cell values so read/write paths share behavior intentionally rather than by proximity.
- Add focused tests for worksheet decoding and encoding rules independently from archive assembly.

Acceptance criteria:
- Structured XLSX read/write logic is decomposed into smaller files/modules by concern.
- Worksheet row logic can be tested without exercising ZIP archive generation.
- Cell coercion/rendering rules live behind dedicated helpers instead of being embedded in the worksheet encoder/decoder loops.

title: Unify preprocessor operator rewriting behind shared scanning rules
description:
The preprocessor’s operator rewriting is only partially declarative. A small config table exists, but several of the most delicate operators still rely on bespoke byte-walking scanners and duplicated precedence logic.

Evidence:
- `internal/preprocessor/transformers_operators.go:31-108` defines declarative configs for some binary operators.
- `internal/preprocessor/transformers_operators.go:168-259` (`as`) and `internal/preprocessor/transformers_operators.go:261-322` (`is`) duplicate string scanning and left-operand extraction patterns.
- `internal/preprocessor/transformers_operators.go:344-417` (`**`) implements a completely separate right-operand scanner.
- `internal/preprocessor/preprocessor.go:133-240` drives a long ordered chain of `handleX()` calls, which means precedence and interaction rules are encoded procedurally rather than described in one place.

Why this matters:
- Adding or changing operators requires understanding several scanner styles and subtle ordering constraints.
- Similar bugs can recur in different operator implementations because the parsing patterns are duplicated.
- The current design hides precedence decisions inside control flow, which raises review cost and makes regressions harder to predict.

Suggested direction:
- Move operator definitions toward a single declarative model (precedence, associativity, operand scanning rules, rewrite form).
- Extract shared operand-scanning helpers for typed operators (`as`, `is`) and infix operators that need custom right-boundary logic.
- Add focused tests around precedence interactions so new operators do not depend on handler ordering alone.

Acceptance criteria:
- `as`, `is`, exponent, and generic binary operators share common scanning infrastructure.
- Operator precedence/stop conditions are documented in one place.
- New operator additions do not require editing multiple unrelated scanning loops.

title: Reject multiple stdin-backed CLI inputs instead of silently returning nil on later reads
description:
`internal/io/input.go` reads `os.Stdin` every time a source starts with `:`. After the first stdin-backed input drains the stream, later stdin-backed inputs receive empty content, and `formats.Read("", mimeType)` returns `nil` without an error.

Evidence:
- Repro: `printf \{"a":1}' | go run ./cmd/infomunge -s json -i extra=:json %im 0.1
output application/json
---
{payload: payload, extra: extra}`
- Actual output: `{"extra":null,"payload":{"a":1}}`

Why this is risky:
- The second stdin consumer looks valid but evaluates as `null`, so users can get corrupted results without any explicit failure.
- The same silent behavior is possible with repeated `-i name=:format` flags.

Code references:
- `internal/cli/app.go:90-97`
- `internal/io/input.go:26-44`
- `pkg/formats/reader.go:15-18`

Expected:
- Either reject multiple stdin-backed inputs up front, or buffer stdin once and fan it out intentionally.

title: Native builds cannot load embedded dw::core modules outside repo-root layouts
description:
Problem

The native (non-JS) module loader only resolves imports from filesystem search paths under the script base directory. It never falls back to the embedded `dw::core` module sources, even though those sources are already embedded in `modules/dw/core/sources.go` and the JS loader handles them specially.

Reproduction

1. Build the CLI: `go build -o tmp/infomunge ./cmd/infomunge`
2. Create `tmp/standard-core.im`:
   `%im 0.1`
   `output application/json`
   `import * from dw::core::Arrays`
   `---`
   `countBy([1,2,3], (x) -> x > 1)`
3. Run `./tmp/infomunge -f tmp/standard-core.im`
4. Observe: `module "dw::core::Arrays" not found (searched in [.../tmp .../tmp/modules])`

Expected

`dw::core::*` imports should work from an installed/native binary regardless of where the script lives. The embedded standard modules already exist in the binary and should not depend on repo-relative files being present.

Why this matters

Right now built-in module support is accidentally tied to the repo layout. Scripts that work from the repo root fail when the binary is used from another directory, which breaks portability for the CLI and undermines the value of embedding those module sources.

Code references

- `internal/runner/module_loader.go:23-94`
- `modules/dw/core/sources.go:9-38`
- `internal/runner/module_loader_js.go:27-60` (already has the desired standard-module fallback behavior)

Acceptance criteria

- Teach the non-JS loader to resolve/load standard modules before filesystem lookup.
- Add regression coverage for running a native binary against a script outside the repo root that imports `dw::core::*`.

title: Centralize output formatting policy across CLI HTTP and WASM
description:
Fresh-eyes cohesion/coupling audit finding.

Problem:
XML output formatting policy is duplicated across runner, HTTP/WASM handlers, and test harness code. Namespace extraction, output option application, and XML writer selection are spread across packages, causing policy drift and forcing adapters to know runner context internals.

Evidence:
- `internal/runner/runner.go` defines `ContextKeyNamespaces`, `ContextKeyOutputOptions`, `ExtractNamespaceVars`, `ApplyXMLOutputOptions`, and XML-specific logic inside `formatOutputWithContext`.
- `internal/handlers/run.go` repeats the same XML path in `FormatRunResult` and imports runner solely to access context keys/helpers.
- `test/godog_test.go` has local copies of XML formatting helper logic around the runner output path.
- `pkg/formats` owns `XMLOutputOptions`, but parsing/applying header output options lives in runner.

Suggested direction:
- Introduce a single output formatting component, for example `internal/output` or a narrowly scoped `runner.FormatExecutionResult`.
- Give it a typed metadata struct instead of magic context keys (`__namespaces__`, `__output_options__`).
- Keep XML option parsing/application in one place and have CLI, server, WASM, and tests call that same function.

Acceptance criteria:
- XML namespace and output-option handling has one production implementation.
- `internal/handlers` no longer reaches into runner context-key constants for formatting policy.
- Test harness uses the same formatting path as production instead of helper copies.
- Add cucumber coverage for at least one XML namespace/options scenario through `/run` or WASM-compatible handler flow plus existing CLI output behavior.

title: Stabilize flaky go test all regression feature around lambda stringification
description:
`test/features/go_test_all_regression.feature` currently fails intermittently because `internal/testing/properties.TestEvaluate_NoPanics_Deterministic_AndTypeConsistent` can treat lambda-containing results as nondeterministic.

Observed on April 19, 2026 while verifying `bd-2abm`:
- `go test ./...` failed inside the cucumber scenario.
- The failing generated expression concatenated a string with an array containing a lambda.
- The two evaluations differed only by lambda pointer addresses embedded in the formatted string output.

Example symptom:
- first: `"s[7 0.08718961160566452 0x... cj [<nil> map[D_32110:-25] true]]"`
- second: `"s[7 0.08718961160566452 0x... cj [<nil> map[D_32110:-25] true]]"`

Follow-up work:
- Make lambda stringification deterministic, or
- Teach the property generator / determinism check to avoid this false nondeterminism path, and
- Re-run `test/features/go_test_all_regression.feature` until it is stable.

title: Split format registry from bundled codec implementations and option dispatch
description:
Problem:
`pkg/formats` contains the public read/write registry, MIME and extension lookup, XML namespace rendering, option dispatch, and all codecs including protobuf, XLSX, Java serialization, multipart, flatfile, CSV, JSON, YAML, and XML. Registering a new option-aware format requires editing central maps in `options_dispatch.go`.

Why it matters:
The package has low cohesion and high compile-time coupling: importing the registry brings every codec and heavy transitive dependency into the same package. It makes the format boundary harder to extract as a library and increases the chance that a format-specific change affects unrelated format behavior.

Evidence:
- `pkg/formats/registry.go` owns global readers/writers/extensions.
- `pkg/formats/options_dispatch.go` is a central list of option-aware codecs.
- `pkg/formats/protobuf*.go`, `xlsx*.go`, `xml.go`, `flatfile.go`, `java.go`, and the light codecs all share one package and init-time registration.

Suggested direction:
Keep a small formats core package for value aliases, registry interfaces, MIME normalization, and option registration. Move heavier codecs into subpackages or registration modules that explicitly install themselves. Let each codec register its own option handlers with the registry instead of editing a central dispatch map.

Acceptance:
- Adding a new option-aware format does not require changing a central options dispatch file.
- Lightweight registry/value tests can run without compiling every codec implementation.
- Existing format behavior remains covered by current reader/writer tests and relevant cucumber features.

title: Fix malformed embedded playground CSS selector for toolbar controls
description:
The embedded playground stylesheet contains malformed CSS selector syntax in `internal/cli/webapp.go`, which can break toolbar input/select styling and make UI behavior browser-dependent.

Evidence:
- `internal/cli/webapp.go:65-66`
  - `.toolbar select {`
  - `.toolbar input {`
- Missing comma/brace creates an invalid rule block.

Impact:
- Styles for toolbar form controls are not reliably applied.
- Playground appearance can regress silently without compile-time checks because HTML/CSS is embedded as a raw Go string.

Proposed fix:
- Correct the selector block to a valid grouped selector (`.toolbar select, .toolbar input { ... }`).
- Add a lightweight test/lint check for critical embedded HTML/CSS template validity (or extract template assets for tooling coverage).

title: Unicode string indexing builtins use byte offsets instead of rune indices
description:
Adversarial expression audit found inconsistent Unicode indexing across string builtins.

Repros on current @:
- `charAt("é", 0)` returns `"Ã"` instead of `"é"`
- `charAt("é", 1)` returns `"©"` instead of an out-of-range error
- `charAt("😀", 0)` returns `"ð"`
- `indexOf("éx", "x")` returns `2` instead of `1`
- `lastIndexOf("aéé", "é")` returns `3` instead of `2`
- Combined inconsistency: `[substring("éx", 0, 1), indexOf("éx", "x"), charAt("éx", 1)]` currently evaluates to `["é", 2, "©"]`

Likely root cause:
- `internal/evaluator/builtins_string_basic.go:145-149` uses `len(str)` and `str[idx]` in `charAt`, so it indexes bytes rather than runes.
- `internal/evaluator/builtins_string_basic.go:203-209` and `230-236` delegate string `indexOf`/`lastIndexOf` to `strings.Index` / `strings.LastIndex`, which return byte offsets.
- This conflicts with the surrounding API behavior: `substring` and `charCodeAt` are already implemented in rune space (`internal/evaluator/builtins_string_basic.go:105-126` and `169-174`).

Coverage gap:
- Existing cucumber coverage exercises ASCII-only `charAt`/`indexOf`/`lastIndexOf` cases in `test/features/string_functions_additional.feature:352-555`.
- Unicode coverage currently exists for `substring` in `test/features/string_edge_cases.feature:592-603`, but not for the indexing builtins.

Expected work:
- Make `charAt`, string `indexOf`, and string `lastIndexOf` operate in rune indices/code points.
- Add cucumber regressions covering accented characters and emoji for these builtins.

title: Inconsistent use of type aliases vs raw map[string]interface{}
description:
The evaluator package defines type aliases for clarity:
- `type Value = interface{}`
- `type Context = map[string]interface{}`
- `type Object = map[string]interface{}`
- `type Array = []interface{}`

However, many files — especially `builtins_core.go` (27 occurrences), `declarations.go` (13), `runner.go` (15), and `builtins_collection_ops.go` (27) — use the raw `map[string]interface{}` form instead of the aliases. There are 411 total occurrences of `map[string]interface{}` across 68 Go files.

This inconsistency makes the code harder to read and obscures intent. For example, a function parameter typed `map[string]interface{}` could be an evaluation context, an object value, or output options — the alias would disambiguate.

Migrate call sites to use the type aliases where semantically appropriate.

Files:
- `internal/evaluator/types_value.go` (alias definitions)
- All builtin, runner, and declaration files that use raw types

title: Lazy filter silently skips non-boolean predicate results
Replace gopherjs with WebAssembly for standalone playground
description:
gopherjs is stuck at Go 1.20 and won't build with Go 1.26+. Replace it with a standard WASM build.

## Work required

1. Create cmd/infomunge-wasm/main.go
   - Build tag: //go:build js
   - Use syscall/js instead of github.com/gopherjs/gopherjs/js
   - Expose infomungeRun as a global JS function via js.FuncOf
   - Block main with a channel (select{}) so the wasm module stays alive
   - Same logic as cmd/infomunge-js/main.go: DecodeRunRequest -> BuildRunContext -> RunStringWithGoContextAndOptionsWithOutput -> ResolveOutputMimeType -> FormatRunResult
   - Return map keys: ok (bool), result (string), mimeType (string), error (string)
   - Note: js.ValueOf does not handle map[string]interface{}; build the return js.Value manually or encode as JSON and parse in JS

2. Build step
   - GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm go build -o docs/playground/infomunge.wasm ./cmd/infomunge-wasm

3. Copy wasm_exec.js
   - Source: $(go env GOROOT)/lib/wasm/wasm_exec.js (~17KB)
   - Dest: docs/playground/wasm_exec.js
   - Check into repo so playground works without Go toolchain present
   - Must be re-copied when Go toolchain is upgraded

4. Update docs/playground/index.html
   - Replace <script src="infomunge.js"></script> with:
     <script src="wasm_exec.js"></script>
     <script>
       const go = new Go();
       WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming(fetch('infomunge.wasm'), go.importObject)
         .then(result => go.run(result.instance));
     </script>
   - runScript() already checks window.infomungeRun; no other JS changes needed

5. Add Makefile target playground-wasm

6. Verify with a build-smoke cucumber or unit test

## Notes
- cmd/infomunge-js (gopherjs) can be left in place for historical reference
- js.FuncOf callbacks must not be GC'd; hold refs in package-level vars

title: Fix dw::core::Arrays module import parse failures in go test ./...
description: After fixing bd-3pj3, repo-root go test ./... no longer fails in tmp but still fails in the Godog suite. The remaining failures are in features/arrays_module.feature, where imports of dw::core::Arrays fail with ParseError at line import statements. This appears unrelated to tmp package discovery and should be handled as a separate bug.

title: Bug: << and >> array operators have identical implementation
description:
The `<<` and `>>` operators in `internal/evaluator/evaluator.go` have identical implementations — both append an element to the right side of an array. `appendRight` (>>, line 387) and `arrayAppend` (<<, line 399) produce the same result: `[...array, element]`.

In DataWeave, these operators have distinct semantics. Having two operators that do the same thing is confusing. Either `<<` should prepend (creating `[element, ...array]`), or if both are intentionally append-right, one should be removed or the difference documented.

Test scenarios in `test/features/core_evaluator_runner_coverage.feature:131-179` confirm both produce the same append behavior. The chained test at line 321 (`([1] << 2) >> 3`) also treats them identically.

Files:
- `internal/evaluator/evaluator.go:387-408`
- `test/features/core_evaluator_runner_coverage.feature:131-179`

title: Collapse runner execution APIs into a cohesive facade
description:
Problem:
The runner exposes several overlapping entrypoints and compatibility wrappers: `RunFromStringWithContextAndOptionsAndGoContext`, `RunStringWithGoContextAndOptionsWithOutput`, `ExecuteStringWithGoContextAndOptions`, `FormatExecutionResult`, `PrintExecutionResult`, plus private `evaluate` and `formatOutput` paths. Callers have to choose between raw value, metadata tuple, structured result, formatted string, and stdout side effects.

Why it matters:
This keeps execution, formatting policy, context metadata, stdout behavior, and compatibility concerns coupled in one package. It makes new adapters such as CLI, HTTP, WASM, and tests more likely to pick a subtly different path and drift in behavior.

Evidence:
- `internal/cli/app.go` uses `ExecuteStringWithContextAndOptions` plus `FormatExecutionResult`.
- `internal/cli/server.go` and `cmd/infomunge-wasm/main.go` use `RunStringWithGoContextAndOptionsWithOutput`.
- `internal/runner/runner.go` still owns stdout helpers and deprecated compatibility wrappers.
- `internal/runner/execution.go` already has `ExecutionResult`, suggesting a better single return shape exists.

Suggested direction:
Make `ExecuteString(ctx, script, inputs/options) (ExecutionResult, error)` the main adapter API, then layer thin CLI stdout and compatibility functions around it or retire unused wrappers. Prefer returning `ExecutionResult` over multi-value tuples.

Acceptance:
- CLI, server, WASM, and godog use the same structured execution path.
- Multi-value runner APIs are deprecated or removed when no external callers remain.
- Formatting and printing stay outside the core execution function.

title: Make post-processing pipeline mapping-aware
description:
The post-processing pipeline (CreateModularPostProcessingPipeline in internal/preprocessor/stages.go) runs approximately 40 transform stages after the rewriter phase. These stages (string interpolation, operator rewrites, arrow functions, filter/map/reduce operators, selector processing, syntax transforms) can all change string lengths.

However, ModularPipeline.Execute() only returns a string, not (string, []int). This means the character-level position mapping built by the rewriter is stale for the final output that goes to the Go parser. Error positions reported for expressions that undergo significant post-processing transforms may be approximate rather than exact.

To fix: each PipelineStage.Execute() would need to return (string, []int, error) and each transformHandler would need to produce a mapping. This affects approximately 40 transform functions across stages.go, transformers_syntax.go, transformers_lambda.go, transformers_operators.go, and related files.

title: Support inline if values in one-line object literals
description: While working bd-3ko6, PrepareForParsing rejected one-line object values such as foo: if (true) 1 else 2 when wrapped as a top-level object. The core rewriter branch scanner can treat the object-closing brace as a branch close and report branch scan or brace errors before the intended parse result. Acceptance: add cucumber or unit coverage for object fields whose value is an inline if expression; fix branch scanning so object boundaries terminate the value cleanly without corrupting source maps.

title: Make builtin registration domain-owned and descriptor-based
description:
Fresh-eyes cohesion/coupling audit finding.

Problem:
Builtin registration is centralized in one large evaluator registry even though implementations are split by domain. This creates a high-coupling edit point for every builtin addition and makes metadata like arity, evaluation strategy, module ownership, and docs implicit.

Evidence:
- `internal/evaluator/modular_registry.go` manually lists all special and regular builtins in two large maps.
- Handler functions live across many `builtins_*` files, but each new function still requires editing the central registry.
- Special vs regular evaluation strategy is represented only by which map the name appears in.
- There is no first-class builtin descriptor carrying arity, category/module, laziness, or user-facing docs.

Suggested direction:
- Introduce `BuiltinSpec` descriptors with name, category/module, arity, evaluation mode (eager/special), and handler.
- Let each builtin domain file register or expose its own specs, with the central registry only aggregating slices.
- Keep thread-safe override hooks for tests.

Acceptance criteria:
- Adding a builtin in one domain can be done without editing a giant cross-domain map.
- Registry tests validate duplicate names, invalid specs, and special/eager dispatch.
- Existing builtin lookup APIs continue to work during migration.
- Add a small docs/test helper that can enumerate builtins by category to prove metadata is usable.

title: Improve post-processing mapping precision with per-transform mappings
description:
Current pipeline mapping support is stage-level and uses inferred string alignment between each stage's input/output. This is a major improvement over stale mappings, but it can still be approximate for heavily rewritten middle segments.

Follow-up:
- Add optional exact mapping support to individual transform handlers (for operators/selectors/syntax rewrites with known token edits)
- Prefer exact per-transform composition where available, and fall back to inferred alignment otherwise
- Add focused cucumber scenarios that assert exact columns for representative complex rewrites

title: Split runner execution engine from formatting and IO adapters
description:
Fresh-eyes cohesion/coupling audit finding.

Problem:
`internal/runner` currently owns too many responsibilities at once:
- file reading and base-dir discovery (`Run`, `RunWithConfig`)
- header parsing and context construction (`evaluateWithContext`, `parseHeaderWithGoContext`)
- module loading setup (`NewModuleLoader`)
- preprocessing and source-map composition
- evaluator invocation
- lazy/stream resolution
- output serialization and stdout printing (`formatOutputWithContext`)
- XML-specific output option interpretation (`ApplyXMLOutputOptions`)

This makes the runner the gravitational center for unrelated changes. A change to output formatting, module loading, source-map handling, or evaluation API tends to touch `internal/runner/runner.go`, which increases regression risk and makes library extraction harder.

Evidence:
- `internal/runner/runner.go` is 526 lines and imports evaluator, preprocessor, sourcemap, stringutils, formats, os, filepath, strconv, and fmt.
- The public runner API has overlapping entrypoints (`RunFromStringWithContextAndOptions`, `RunStringWithGoContextAndOptionsWithOutput`, `RunStringWithGoContext`, etc.) that expose internal pipeline shape rather than a cohesive execution result.
- `formatOutputWithContext` prints to stdout directly, while other adapters need returned strings.

Suggested direction:
- Introduce a small execution service/API that returns a structured `ExecutionResult` containing value, header/output metadata, eval context, and source-map-aware errors.
- Move stdout/file adapters to CLI-facing code.
- Move result resolution and output serialization behind explicit collaborators rather than keeping them in runner.
- Preserve current public functions as compatibility wrappers initially.

Acceptance criteria:
- New internal API can evaluate a script without printing or formatting.
- CLI output path is an adapter over that API.
- Existing runner entrypoints remain behavior-compatible or have focused migration notes.
- Add/adjust cucumber coverage for CLI output plus an in-process runner path to catch behavior drift.

title: Split structured protobuf format support into smaller modules
description:
`pkg/formats/protobuf_structured.go` is carrying too many responsibilities in one 1.5k-line file: option parsing, schema construction from two sources, descriptor traversal, raw wire decoding, raw wire encoding, map-entry handling, packed-field support, and number coercion helpers.

Evidence:
- `pkg/formats/protobuf_structured.go:80-215` handles option parsing plus descriptor-backed schema construction.
- `pkg/formats/protobuf_structured.go:290-544` builds schema objects from descriptors and schema literals.
- `pkg/formats/protobuf_structured.go:547-861` performs decode-time wire parsing, including map-entry handling.
- `pkg/formats/protobuf_structured.go:863-1173` performs encode-time wire generation with large kind switches.
- `pkg/formats/protobuf_structured.go:1175-1507` contains low-level wire skipping and numeric conversion helpers.

Why this matters:
- There is no narrow seam for reviewing or testing changes to just schema handling, decoding, or encoding.
- The same domain concepts (`protobufField`, wire types, strictness rules) are touched by distant sections of the same file, increasing change risk.
- Future features like enum names, unknown-field preservation, or oneof support will compound the existing file-level complexity.

Suggested direction:
- Split this implementation into smaller files/modules by concern: options/schema, descriptor import, decoder, encoder, wire helpers/conversions.
- Introduce targeted tests per layer instead of relying on large end-to-end coverage only.
- Consider small internal types/interfaces that make encode/decode rules composable without sharing one giant switch surface.

Acceptance criteria:
- Structured protobuf logic is split into smaller units with clear ownership boundaries.
- Decoder and encoder logic can be tested independently from schema parsing.
- Numeric coercion and wire helper code are isolated from high-level format option handling.

title: Extract embedded playground HTML from Go string to go:embed file
description:
The entire playground HTML/CSS/JS (558 lines) is embedded as a raw string constant in `internal/cli/webapp.go`. This makes it impossible to:

- Lint or format the HTML/CSS/JS with standard tools
- Test the frontend code independently
- Get syntax highlighting or editor support when editing the UI
- Run security scanners on the client-side JavaScript

Go's `embed` directive (`//go:embed`) would allow the HTML to live in a proper `.html` file while still being compiled into the binary. The standalone WASM playground already uses separate HTML files in `docs/playground/`.

Consider extracting to `internal/cli/playground.html` with `//go:embed playground.html` and keeping the same server behavior.

Files:
- `internal/cli/webapp.go` (558 lines, all one string constant)

title: Unify script header and module directive parsing
description:
Fresh-eyes cohesion/coupling audit finding.

Problem:
Script header parsing and module parsing duplicate directive recognition and declaration application. The two paths have subtly different control flow, offset accounting, context updates, and supported directives, which makes grammar changes expensive and risky.

Evidence:
- `internal/runner/header_directives.go` parses directives into `headerDirective` values and applies them through `applyHeaderDirective`.
- `internal/runner/module_parser.go` independently loops over lines, switches on the same directive prefixes, calls many of the same declaration helpers, and maintains its own offset/line-context handling.
- `internal/runner/declarations.go` has declaration parsing/evaluation helpers shared by both, but orchestration still lives in two places.

Suggested direction:
- Extract a shared declaration/directive parser that can run in script-header mode and module-header mode.
- Model mode-specific policy explicitly, e.g. whether `output`, `input`, namespace declarations, imports, and `---` are allowed.
- Return typed declarations plus source spans, then have separate applicators for script context and module namespace.

Acceptance criteria:
- Adding a new header/module declaration requires changing one parser, not separate script and module loops.
- Module mode still rejects `---` with source context.
- Existing import, var, fun, and type behavior remains covered by focused tests.
- Add cucumber or runner/module tests proving a multiline `var` or `fun` behaves consistently in script headers and modules.

title: Finish pulling preprocessor rewrites into explicit transform stages
description:
Problem:
`PrepareForParsing` still has a bespoke flow before the contract pipeline: comment stripping, regex replacement, implicit object wrapping, top-level object wrapping, the stateful rewriter, recursive second-pass if handling, and only then `CreateModularPostProcessingPipelineWithOptions`. The rewriter itself has a hard-coded handler order in `RewriteWithDepth`.

Why it matters:
Syntax behavior, source-map composition, and transform ordering are spread across `preprocessor.go`, `rewriter_handlers.go`, `stages.go`, and the transform files. New syntax changes have to reason about two transformation systems and multiple mapping composition points.

Evidence:
- `internal/preprocessor/preprocessor.go` composes regex, wrapping, rewriter, and post-pipeline mappings manually.
- `internal/preprocessor/rewriter_handlers.go` contains the core if/while/do/update/object-key rewrite order.
- `internal/preprocessor/stages.go` exposes `TransformContract` ordering only for post-rewriter transforms.

Suggested direction:
Represent the pre-rewriter wrappers and core rewriter as named transform contracts or phase objects with explicit mapping mode and order. Keep the byte-walking rewriter if needed, but make it a stage in the same pipeline contract and trace output.

Acceptance:
- `TraceTransforms` includes every transform that can change source text.
- There is one documented transform order for the full preprocess path.
- Source-map tests cover at least one failure position through regex/wrap/rewriter/post-pipeline composition.

title: Separate evaluator scope from runtime capabilities and output metadata
description:
Problem:
`evaluator.Context` is currently `map[string]Value` and is used for user bindings plus runtime services and adapter metadata. Examples include `__go_ctx__`, `__deadline`, `__format_service__`, `__url_read_service__`, `__output_metadata__`, and `__input_mime__`.

Why it matters:
This couples evaluator, runner, output, CLI/HTTP adapters, and IO services through magic string keys. It makes user namespace collision behavior implicit, makes lambda context copying need to know runtime capabilities, and weakens the library extraction goal in README.md.

Evidence:
- `internal/evaluator/types_value.go` stores Go context and deadline in `Context`.
- `internal/evaluator/io_capabilities.go` stores format and URL services in `Context`.
- `internal/output/output.go` stores XML/output metadata in `Context`.
- `internal/runner/execution.go` merges header/additional bindings and installs capabilities into the same map.

Suggested direction:
Introduce a typed execution scope, for example `Scope{Vars, Capabilities, OutputMetadata}`, or keep `evaluator.Context` only for user/module symbols and pass services/metadata through typed evaluator/run options. Add guardrails for reserved names.

Acceptance:
- User/module bindings are separated from non-user runtime metadata.
- Lambda/function context copying no longer needs a hard-coded hidden-key list.
- Existing CLI, server, WASM, and module declaration behavior stays covered by cucumber or focused Go tests.

title: Keep scratch Go programs under tmp from breaking go test ./...
description:
A plain `go test ./...` from the repo root currently fails because scratch programs in `tmp/` are treated as part of module package `infomunge/tmp`, and multiple files define `main`.

Evidence:
- Command: `go test ./...`
- Failure includes:
  - `tmp/inspect_dkes.go:8:6: main redeclared in this block`
  - `tmp/inspect_dkes2.go:9:6: main redeclared in this block`
  - `tmp/repro_dkes.go:9:6: main redeclared in this block`
  - `tmp/repro_tmjo.go:9:6: main redeclared in this block`
  - `tmp/test_preprocessor.go:8:6: main redeclared in this block`

Why this matters:
- It breaks the standard Go quality gate and makes it harder to trust quick verification commands during development and review.

Possible fixes:
- Move scratch programs outside the module package tree
- Add build tags so ad hoc helpers are excluded from normal test/package discovery
- Standardize on a single helper entrypoint instead of accumulating multiple `package main` files in `tmp/`

Code / repo references:
- `tmp/inspect.go`
- `tmp/inspect_dkes.go`
- `tmp/inspect_dkes2.go`
- `tmp/repro_dkes.go`
- `tmp/repro_tmjo.go`
- `tmp/test_preprocessor.go`

title: Centralize source mapping and diagnostic offset handling
description:
The source-location mapping logic is spread across the preprocessor, runner, and evaluator, with hand-adjusted offsets in multiple places.

Evidence:
- `internal/preprocessor/preprocessor.go:32-64` mutates the mapping after top-level object wrapping with bespoke index rewriting.
- `internal/runner/runner.go:159-181` threads `bodyOffset`, raw source, and preprocessor mappings into evaluation.
- `internal/runner/declarations.go:45-53`, `internal/runner/declarations.go:130-140`, and `internal/runner/runner.go:481-506` compute offsets manually for declaration and header diagnostics.
- `internal/evaluator/evaluator.go:76-185` contains separate parse-error and eval-error remapping paths that depend on those offsets staying aligned.

Why this matters:
- Small syntax rewrites can silently break line/column reporting because mapping assumptions are duplicated.
- Error-reporting fixes become invasive: any change to preprocessing, header normalization, or declaration parsing can affect diagnostics.
- This code is difficult to reason about because the mapping contract is implicit rather than represented as a dedicated type.

Suggested direction:
- Introduce a dedicated source-map type with clear invariants and helpers for composition, slicing, and offset shifting.
- Stop open-coding byte-offset math in runner declaration parsing.
- Add focused tests that assert stable diagnostics across header/body rewrites.

Acceptance criteria:
- Mapping transformations and offset shifts are centralized behind a dedicated API.
- Header/body/declaration callers use shared helpers instead of manual arithmetic.
- Regression tests cover representative rewrites (`if/else`, object wrapping, multiline `var`/`fun`) and verify original source positions.

title: Refactor runner header parsing into a parse-first pipeline
description:
The runner header path mixes parsing, preprocessing, evaluation, module loading, context mutation, and source-offset bookkeeping in one flow.

Evidence:
- `internal/runner/runner.go:153-186` evaluates the body immediately after header parsing and threads raw source, body offsets, and preprocessor mappings through the same path.
- `internal/runner/runner.go:325-520` stores mutable parser state (`context`, `namespaces`, `outputMimeType`, `headerOffset`, `fullRaw`, `loader`, `goCtx`) and drives directives through closure-based registrations.
- `internal/runner/declarations.go:20-58`, `internal/runner/declarations.go:68-145`, and `internal/runner/declarations.go:193-217` duplicate the work of parse -> preprocess -> evaluate/compile for variable and function declarations.

Why this matters:
- Adding a new directive currently means reasoning about parsing semantics, evaluation order, and diagnostics at the same time.
- The coupling makes regression scope large whenever header behavior changes.
- Unit-testing directive parsing in isolation is harder than it should be because evaluation is embedded in the parser path.

Suggested direction:
- Introduce an explicit header AST / directive model.
- Parse directives first, then evaluate declarations/imports in a second pass.
- Move line-offset/error-context handling behind a smaller interface so directive handlers are not responsible for source bookkeeping.

Acceptance criteria:
- Header parsing can be tested without invoking evaluator execution for every directive.
- `fun`, `var`, `type`, `import`, `ns`, and `output` handling no longer rely on closure registrations mutating shared parse state directly.
- Existing header diagnostics remain covered by focused tests.

description:
Standalone playground now boots from wasm (`wasm_exec.js` + `infomunge.wasm`), but legacy `docs/playground/infomunge.js` and `docs/playground/infomunge.js.map` still exist and may cause confusion.

title: Redundant error wrapping in app.go duplicates error message
User-defined functions ignore captured lexical scope and can be caller-shadowed
description:
Problem

User-defined functions do not use their definition environment at call time. `buildFunLambda` stores `Env`, but `callUserDefinedFunctionWithVisitor` ignores it and instead copies the caller context. That makes imported functions / closures dynamically scoped and lets caller variables shadow module-local values.

Reproduction

1. Create `tmp/modules/Shadow.im`:
   `%im 0.1`
   `var offset = 5`
   `fun addOffset(x) = x + offset`
2. Create `tmp/shadow-scope.im`:
   `%im 0.1`
   `import modules::Shadow`
   `var offset = 100`
   `output application/json`
   `---`
   `Shadow::addOffset(10)`
3. Run `./tmp/infomunge -f tmp/shadow-scope.im`
4. Observe current output: `110`

Expected

The imported function should evaluate against the module scope it was defined in, so the result should stay `15` even when the caller defines its own `offset`.

Why this matters

This is a real semantic bug, not just an implementation detail. Any imported function or closure that refers to surrounding variables can silently change behavior based on the caller's locals. That makes module APIs brittle and will break future closure-heavy features.

Code references

- `internal/runner/declarations.go:235-240` stores `Env` on `Lambda`
- `internal/evaluator/visitor.go:270-296` ignores `lambda.Env` and copies the caller `context` instead

Acceptance criteria

- Call user-defined functions from their captured lexical environment, then bind parameters on top of that environment.
- Decide explicitly how much of the caller context should remain visible, if any, and document that rule.
- Add coverage for module-variable shadowing and for lambda/function closure capture.

title: Track sourcemap coverage for early preprocessor transforms
description: replaceRegexLiterals and wrapImplicitObjectLiteralBodies still run before the main mapped rewriter, so future diagnostic regressions in those transforms should move onto the shared sourcemap pipeline too.

title: Expand builtin arg-validation helper into declarative wrappers
description: This ticket introduced shared requireExactArgs/requireMinArgs helpers and migrated math/runtime/string builtins. Remaining builtins still repeat argument count and type assertion boilerplate. Follow up by adding declarative wrapper helpers for common signatures (no args, unary string, unary number, binary string/string, etc.) and migrate additional builtin families incrementally while preserving existing error messages and cucumber coverage.

title: Decouple evaluator value model from format and IO packages
description:
Fresh-eyes cohesion/coupling audit finding.

Problem:
Evaluator value types and format-layer types are coupled in both directions of responsibility. The evaluator imports `pkg/formats` for `Namespace` and `XMLMultiValue`, while IO builtins call `formats.Read/Format` directly. This blurs the boundary between language semantics and serialization adapters and works against the README goal that domain logic can be extracted as a library.

Evidence:
- `internal/evaluator/types_value.go` aliases `XMLMultiValue = formats.XMLMultiValue` and treats `formats.Namespace` as an evaluator kind.
- `internal/evaluator/types.go` checks/coerces `formats.Namespace`.
- `internal/evaluator/builtins_io.go` directly owns `read`, `write`, and `readUrl` behavior using `pkg/formats`, HTTP, DNS validation, and response limits.
- `pkg/formats` defines its own `Object`/`Array` aliases that mirror evaluator values, which hides rather than removes the shared value-model dependency.

Suggested direction:
- Define a core value model in a package that is intentionally shared by evaluator and formats, or move namespace/multivalue concepts out of `pkg/formats` if they are language-level values.
- Keep serialization and network IO behind interfaces injected into evaluator builtins or registered as optional capabilities.
- Separate pure evaluation from environmental IO so embedders can use the evaluator without pulling in all format/network behavior.

Acceptance criteria:
- Evaluator no longer needs to import XML/serialization implementation packages for core value kinds.
- `read`/`write` builtins use an explicit format service boundary.
- `readUrl` is isolated as an IO capability with tests for disabled/unavailable environments.
- Existing format and IO cucumber coverage remains behavior-compatible.

title: Duplicated XML output helpers in runner.go and handlers/run.go
description:
Both `internal/runner/runner.go` and `internal/handlers/run.go` contain near-identical implementations of:

1. `extractNamespaceVars` / `ExtractNamespaceVars` — iterate context map looking for `formats.Namespace` values
2. `applyXMLOutputOptions` / `ApplyXMLOutputOptions` — apply raw string options to `XMLOutputOptions`

The handlers version exports these functions (uppercase), while the runner version keeps them unexported. The runner's `formatOutputWithContext` and the handlers' `FormatRunResult` both format XML output using the same pattern: extract namespaces, apply options, call `formats.FormatXMLWithOptions`.

This shared XML output formatting logic should live in one place. The handlers package already exports the helpers — the runner should call them instead of maintaining duplicates.

Files:
- `internal/runner/runner.go:478-516` (unexported versions)
- `internal/handlers/run.go:140-179` (exported versions)

title: Duplicated stripLineComments implementations in preprocessor and declarations
description:
Both `internal/preprocessor/preprocessor.go` and `internal/runner/declarations.go` define their own `stripLineComments` and `stripSingleLineComment` functions. The preprocessor version uses `ScanState` for string tracking, while the declarations version uses manual `inString`/`stringChar`/`escaped` booleans.

These are independently maintained implementations of the same logic that could diverge silently. The preprocessor version also calls `isRegexContext`/`parseRegexLiteral`, while the declarations version calls the exported `preprocessor.IsRegexContext`/`preprocessor.ParseRegexLiteral`.

Consolidate into a single shared implementation — likely in `internal/stringutils` or within the preprocessor package with an exported function.

Files:
- `internal/preprocessor/preprocessor.go:314-346`
- `internal/runner/declarations.go:436-485`

title: Remove evaluator dependency on preprocessor for nested expressions
description:
Problem:
The main architecture is runner preprocesses source, then evaluator executes the parsed expression. That layering is inverted inside evaluator builtins: `builtins_arrays_do.go` and `builtins_update.go` import `internal/preprocessor`, preprocess quoted expression strings at runtime, parse them with `go/parser`, and then evaluate the resulting AST.

Why it matters:
Evaluator behavior now depends directly on source rewrite rules and preprocessor options. Nested expression semantics can drift from top-level semantics, source-map handling becomes harder, and the evaluator cannot be treated as a clean AST/runtime layer.

Evidence:
- `internal/evaluator/builtins_arrays_do.go` calls `preprocessor.PrepareForParsing` for do-block expressions and declarations.
- `internal/evaluator/builtins_update.go` calls `preprocessor.PrepareForParsing` for update case expressions.
- `internal/preprocessor/rewriter_handlers.go` emits `__do` and `__updateExpr` calls with quoted source fragments that the evaluator later reparses.

Suggested direction:
Move nested expression compilation behind a typed boundary. Options include compiling do/update bodies during preprocessing into AST-compatible calls, introducing an evaluator-injected `ExpressionCompiler` interface owned by runner, or creating a shared parser/compiler package that both runner and nested-expression features use without evaluator importing preprocessor directly.

Acceptance:
- `internal/evaluator` no longer imports `internal/preprocessor`.
- Top-level, do-block, and update-expression preprocessing use the same option and source-map policy.
- Existing do/update cucumber and unit coverage still passes, with at least one nested syntax regression test added.

title: Remove over-extracted trivial constants from constants.go
description:
`internal/evaluator/constants.go` extracts trivially obvious numeric literals into named constants that add indirection without aiding readability:

- `ParityDivisor = 2` (used for `n % 2`)
- `DecimalBase = 10` (used in `strconv.FormatInt(..., 10)`)
- `FloatBitSize = 64` (used in `strconv.ParseFloat(..., 64)`)
- `BoolTrueAsInt = 1`, `BoolFalseAsInt = 0`
- `SpaceCharacter = ' '`
- `FirstMonthOfYear = 1`, `FirstDayOfMonth = 1`
- `SundayWeekday = 0`, `DaysInWeek = 7`

These are universally understood values. Wrapping them in constants forces readers to navigate to the definition just to confirm the obvious. The useful constants in the file (`MaxEvalDepth`, `MaxDeepDepth`, `DefaultLoopTimeout`, `TimeoutCheckInterval`) should stay.

Inline the trivial ones and keep only the non-obvious constants.

Files:
- `internal/evaluator/constants.go:53-85`

title: Give preprocessor transforms explicit contracts and ordering
description:
Fresh-eyes cohesion/coupling audit finding.

Problem:
The preprocessor combines a byte-level recursive rewriter with a large fixpoint post-processing pipeline of independent string transformers. Ordering, precedence, mapping accuracy, and termination behavior are encoded implicitly in `stages.go` plus many `replace*` functions, so adding syntax requires understanding the whole pipeline.

Evidence:
- `internal/preprocessor/preprocessor.go` does comment stripping, regex replacement, object wrapping, recursive rewrite, then `CreateModularPostProcessingPipeline`.
- `internal/preprocessor/stages.go` contains long ordered transform lists, including loops over operator and functional transforms with independent iteration guards.
- Many transforms use inferred mappings via `inferStageMapping`; only some provide exact mappings.
- Prior mistakes in `MIND_MAP.md` repeatedly mention preprocessor regressions from scanner ordering, broad patches, multiline parsing assumptions, and mapping/transform fragility.

Suggested direction:
- Define a transform contract with explicit metadata: name, phase, precedence/associativity where relevant, exact mapping support, and idempotence/loop expectations.
- Split lexical scanning/tokenization concerns from syntactic rewrites where possible.
- Prefer table-driven binary/operator transforms for common cases instead of bespoke `replace*` functions.
- Add a preprocessor debug trace option to show phase-by-phase output for failing syntax cases.

Acceptance criteria:
- There is a documented transform lifecycle and ordering rule in code or docs.
- New operator additions can use a shared path for precedence/scanning/mapping instead of custom pipeline surgery.
- At least one existing operator family is migrated to the new contract as a proving slice.
- Cucumber or unit tests verify source-map error locations for a migrated transform.

title: Consolidate duplicate cucumber test scenarios across feature files
description:
Multiple cucumber feature files contain identical test scenarios with the same names and assertions. Examples include:

- "sum basic usage" in aggregation_functions.feature and math_functions.feature
- "mod basic usage" in math_functions.feature and utility_functions.feature
- "avg basic usage" and "avg with floats" duplicated across files
- "filter Object basic usage" and "filterObject on non-object fails" duplicated
- "log requires exactly one argument", "logWith" scenarios duplicated
- "envVar" scenarios duplicated

There are approximately 30+ duplicated scenario names. Each duplicate runs the same assertion twice, inflating test counts without adding coverage and creating a maintenance burden where changes must be made in multiple places.

Fix: consolidate each scenario to a single canonical location. Choose the most appropriate feature file for each and remove duplicates from the others.

title: Remove empty builtins.go redirect file
Input readers need size limits for stdin, multipart parts, and XLSX ZIP entries
description:
Problem

Several ingestion paths read unbounded data into memory with `io.ReadAll` and do not enforce size or entry-count limits. The obvious cases are CLI stdin, multipart parts, and XLSX ZIP entries.

Examples in code

- `internal/io/input.go:42` reads all stdin into memory
- `pkg/formats/multipart.go:47` reads every multipart part body into memory
- `pkg/formats/xlsx_workbook.go:69-83` reads every ZIP entry into memory with no decompressed-size guard

Why this matters

A large input or crafted archive can drive excessive allocations or OOM the process. XLSX is especially risky because a small compressed file can expand dramatically when decompressed. The server already enforces a 1 MiB request-body cap, but these lower-level readers still have no independent safety rails and can be reached from the CLI and builtins.

Expected

Parsing paths should fail fast with validation errors once they exceed explicit limits (total bytes, per-part bytes, ZIP entry count / decompressed bytes, etc.) rather than consuming unbounded memory.

Acceptance criteria

- Define explicit size limits for stdin-backed inputs and format readers that currently slurp data wholesale.
- Add decompressed-size / entry-count protections for XLSX parsing.
- Add regression tests that assert oversized inputs fail cleanly instead of being fully materialized.

title: CLI -f resolves imported modules relative to cwd instead of the script file

`internal/cli/app.go` reads the script file and then calls `runner.RunFromStringWithContextAndOptions(...)` without setting `RunnerOptions.BaseDir`, so module resolution falls back to `os.Getwd()` instead of the script file's directory.

Code references:
- `internal/cli/app.go:133-141`
- `internal/runner/runner.go:74-83`
- `internal/runner/runner.go:163`

Expected:
- `-f <path>` should resolve relative imports from the script file's directory, matching `runner.RunWithConfig` behavior.

title: Support 'pluck' on Objects with lambda
description:
In DataWeave, 'pluck' can be used on an Object to iterate over keys and values, returning an array. It takes a lambda (value, key, index) -> result.

In InfoMunge, 'pluck' currently seems to only support extracting a field from an array of objects (e.g. 'payload pluck "name"').

Reproduction:
%im 0.1
output application/json
---
{"a": 1, "b": 2} pluck (v, k) -> k

Error: lambda expression requires exactly 2 arguments... (or similar parse error indicating lambda not accepted for pluck)

title: LazyMap/LazyFilter silently drop errors from lambdas
description: LazyMap and LazyFilter currently ignore lambda evaluation errors (continue), which can hide failures and produce partial output. Decide on an error propagation strategy (e.g., emit a control/error value, return a LazyValue that fails on GetValue, or surface via a paired error channel) and update behavior/tests. Ref: internal/evaluator/lazy.go:23-67.

title: Intensive Expression Testing
description: Implement grammar-aware property-based testing, mutation testing, and differential testing for infomunge expressions using the rapid library. Goal: greatly improve robustness without manually authoring large numbers of test expressions. See docs/intensive_expression_testing_proposal.md for the full proposal.

title: Add rapid dependency
description: Add pgregory.net/rapid (v1.2.0+) as a test dependency via go get. Verify it compiles and a trivial rapid.Check test passes. This is the foundation library for all property-based and fuzz testing work.

title: Add collection operator and lambda generators
description:
Create internal/testing/exprgen/collections.go with generators for:

- Collection operators: map, filter, reduce, flatMap applied to array expressions
- Lambda expressions: (param) -> expr and (param, index) -> expr forms
- Implicit dollar-sign lambda: $ and $$ references
- The generator must track lambda parameter names in scope so that nested lambdas reference the correct variables

Update ExprGen to include CollectionOpGen and LambdaGen. Add self-tests verifying generated collection expressions parse correctly.

title: Add conditional, default, string interpolation, and builtin call generators
description:
Expand the expression generator to support:

- Conditional: if (expr) expr else expr
- Default operator: expr default expr
- String interpolation: "text $(expr) text"
- Builtin function calls: builtin(expr, ...) for a subset of builtins: sizeOf, typeOf, upper, lower, flatten, keys, values, trim, isEmpty, contains, startsWith, endsWith
- Case expression: case expr { pattern => expr, ... } (stretch — add if straightforward)

Each builtin call generator should respect the function's arity. Add generator self-tests.

title: Add remaining binary operators to generator
description:
Expand the operator generator to include the full operator set:

- Arithmetic: **, % (in addition to existing +, -, *, /)
- Comparison: <=, >= (in addition to existing <, >, ==, !=)
- String/array concatenation: ++
- Regex match: ~=
- Logical: complete set (&&, || already exist)

Update operator weights so common operators are exercised more frequently than rare ones. Add self-tests.

title: Implement algebraic property tests
description:
Create internal/testing/properties/properties_test.go with algebraic property tests:

Arithmetic identities (generate numeric x):
- x + 0 == x
- x * 1 == x
- x * 0 == 0
- x ** 1 == x

Commutativity (generate numeric a, b):
- a + b == b + a
- a * b == b * a

Associativity (generate small numeric a, b, c — use tolerance for floats):
- (a + b) + c == a + (b + c)

Default operator (generate arbitrary x, y):
- x default x == x
- x default y == x when x is non-null
- null default y == y

Boolean logic (generate boolean x):
- !(!x) == x
- x && true == x
- x || false == x

Collection identity (generate array arr):
- arr map (x) -> x == arr
- arr filter (x) -> true == arr

Concatenation (generate array arr):
- [] ++ arr == arr
- arr ++ [] == arr

String operations (generate string s):
- upper(lower(s)) preserves length
- sizeOf(s) >= 0

Each property test uses rapid.Check. Build full infomunge scripts for each property and evaluate via the runner.

title: Implement structural property tests
description:
Create internal/testing/properties/roundtrip_test.go with structural and round-trip property tests:

Structural properties (generate arrays/objects with the expression generator):
- sizeOf(arr map f) == sizeOf(arr) for any non-erroring f
- sizeOf(arr filter f) <= sizeOf(arr)
- sizeOf(flatten(arr)) >= sizeOf(arr) for arrays of arrays
- sizeOf(keys(obj)) == sizeOf(values(obj))

Round-trip property (generate JSON-safe values):
- read(write(val, 'json'), 'application/json') == val

Stability property:
- Byte-identical output when the same expression+input is evaluated multiple times in sequence

Each test uses rapid.Check with the expression and context generators. Verify these properties hold across thousands of generated cases.

title: Implement coverage-guided fuzz targets
description:
Bridge the expression generator to Go's native fuzzer via rapid.MakeFuzz.

Create internal/testing/properties/fuzz_test.go with:

1. FuzzExprEval — generates expressions at depth 3, evaluates with sample context, checks:
   - No panics (implicit via recover)
   - Successful results are JSON-serializable
   - Type consistency
2. FuzzExprPreprocess — generates expressions, runs through preprocessor only, checks no panics
3. FuzzExprDeep — generates expressions at depth 5-6 for deeper exploration

Usage: go test -fuzz=FuzzExprEval -fuzztime=10m ./internal/testing/properties/

Note on rapid.MakeFuzz: rapid provides structured generation within Go's fuzz infrastructure. The coverage guidance comes from Go's fuzzer driving the byte stream; rapid interprets the bytes into structured expressions. This means most exploration hits valid expressions rather than random byte noise.

Add a testdata/fuzz/ directory for corpus persistence across runs.

title: Build cucumber corpus extractor
description:
Create internal/testing/mutation/extractor.go:

Parse .feature files under test/features/ to extract expression/input/expected-output triples:
- Extract the script text from 'When infomunge processes' steps
- Extract input payloads from 'Given input payload is' steps (and named inputs)
- Extract expected outputs from 'Then' steps
- Store as a structured corpus: []CorpusEntry{Script, Inputs, ExpectedOutput, SourceFile, ScenarioName}

ExtractCorpus(featuresDir) returns all entries. This is a one-time extraction that can be re-run as the test suite grows.

Include unit tests that run against the actual test/features/ directory and verify the extractor finds a reasonable number of entries (sanity check).

title: Build expression mutation engine
description:
Create internal/testing/mutation/mutator.go with mutation operators that transform infomunge source-level expressions:

Mutation operators:
- OperatorSwap: replace a binary operator with another (+ → -, map → filter, == → !=, etc.)
- LiteralPerturb: change literals (1 → 0, "a" → "", true → false, null → 0)
- SubtreeSwap: exchange subexpressions between two corpus entries (requires basic expression boundary detection)
- ArgManipulate: remove/add/reorder arguments in function calls
- NestWrap: wrap a subexpression in an extra layer (x → [x][0], x → (x))
- ParenMutate: insert or remove parentheses to stress precedence handling
- FunctionSwap: substitute among compatible builtins (same arity)

Mutate(expr string, rng *rand.Rand) returns a mutated expression string. Each mutation operator works at the source text level using simple pattern matching (not full parsing).

MutateN(expr, n, rng) applies n random mutations in sequence.

Include unit tests verifying each operator produces syntactically different output.

title: Implement mutation-based property tests
description:
Create internal/testing/mutation/mutation_test.go:

For each corpus entry extracted from cucumber features:
1. Apply 1-3 random mutations to the expression
2. Evaluate the mutated expression with the original inputs
3. Assert the invariant: mutated expressions should either produce a result or return an error — never panic
4. Optionally check determinism: same mutation evaluated twice gives same result

Use rapid.Check to drive the random mutation selection. Feed any panics or unexpected failures into the failure artifact pipeline (artifact.go + scenario_gen.go).

Run configuration:
- Default: process a random subset of 100 corpus entries per test run (fast CI mode)
- Full soak: process all entries with up to 10 mutations each (local/nightly mode, controlled by env var)

Include a test that verifies the mutation engine produces at least some non-trivial mutations (i.e., not all mutations result in identical expressions).

title: Build DataWeave CLI harness
description:
Create internal/testing/differential/dw_harness.go:

Wrap the DataWeave CLI (dw run -i payload ...) for differential comparison:
- DWAvailable() checks if the dw command is on PATH; all differential tests skip if not
- DWEval(script, inputs) shells out to dw, captures stdout/stderr, returns parsed result or error
- Timeout: 10 seconds per evaluation (dw can hang on invalid input)
- Normalization rules for known divergences between infomunge and DataWeave:
  - Numeric precision: compare with tolerance for floats
  - Null/missing conventions: map known null representation differences
  - Key ordering: compare objects as unordered key-value sets
  - Whitespace/formatting: compare parsed values, not raw strings

StructuralCompare(infomungeResult, dwResult) returns a detailed diff on mismatch.

Include unit tests with mocked dw output to verify normalization and comparison logic.

title: Build literal expression generator
description:
Create internal/testing/exprgen/literals.go with rapid generators for the minimal literal subset:

- Integers (including zero, negatives, large values)
- Floats (including zero, negatives, edge cases like very small/large)
- Strings (including empty, special characters, unicode)
- Booleans (true, false)
- Null

Each generator should produce a valid infomunge source-level string representation. Include unit tests in literals_test.go verifying that generated literals are syntactically valid.

title: Implement differential comparison tests
description:
Create internal/testing/differential/differential_test.go:

- Add a DW-compatible flag to the expression generator: tag each generated expression with whether it uses infomunge-only features (e.g., while loops). Only generate DW-compatible expressions for differential tests.
- For each generated expression+context:
  1. Evaluate in infomunge
  2. Evaluate in DataWeave via the harness
  3. Compare results using StructuralCompare
  4. On mismatch, save failure artifact and log the expression with both results
- Use rapid.Check with moderate iteration count (1000 — dw CLI is slow)
- All tests skip gracefully if dw is not available (t.Skip)

Feed discrepancies into the failure artifact pipeline for triage and potential cucumber scenario generation.

title: Add CI integration for property and fuzz tests
description:
Configure CI-friendly test runs for the intensive testing suite:

Short-budget CI run (must complete in under 60 seconds):
- Property tests with fixed seed and reduced iteration count (e.g., 500 cases)
- Mutation tests on a random subset of 50 corpus entries
- Fuzz test with -fuzztime=30s

Local/nightly soak run:
- Property tests with 50000+ iterations
- Full mutation corpus with 10 mutations each
- Fuzz test with -fuzztime=30m
- Controlled by INTENSIVE_TEST_SOAK=1 environment variable

Corpus management:
- Persist interesting fuzz corpus entries across runs in testdata/fuzz/
- Add testdata/fuzz/ to version control so corpus grows over time
- Add tmp/intensive-testing/ to .gitignore

Add a Makefile target or script for running the soak tests locally.

title: Implement success metrics reporting
description:
Add metrics collection and reporting to the intensive testing suite:

Track and report after each run:
- Unique failures found (count distinct fingerprints)
- Shrink ratio (average minimized expression length / original length, target ≤ 20%)
- Time-to-minimal-repro (wall-clock from detection to shrunk artifact, target < 30s)
- Promoted cucumber regressions (count scenarios in test/features/ originating from intensive testing)
- Coverage deltas (run go test -coverprofile before/after, diff preprocessor + evaluator line coverage)
- Panic rate (count panics per run, target: 0)
- Mutation kill rate (ratio of detected vs undetected non-equivalent mutations)

Output a summary report to stdout at end of test run. Optionally write to tmp/intensive-testing/report.json for trend tracking.

Review metrics after each phase to decide whether to continue investing or redirect effort.

title: Mutation corpus extractor captures non-equality Then assertions as expected output
description:
Extractor currently treats any quoted Then step as ExpectedOutput (e.g. 'Then the output should contain "x"' and 'Then the error should contain "x"'). This pollutes corpus entries with substring/error assertions as if they were exact output expectations.

Scope:
- Restrict expected-output extraction to exact-equality Then steps only (docstring and scalar forms).
- Ignore contain/error/valid-JSON style Then assertions for ExpectedOutput.
- Add regression tests to prevent reintroduction.

title: Build operator expression generator
description:
Create internal/testing/exprgen/operators.go with rapid generators for the minimal operator subset:

- Binary operators: +, -, *, /, ==, !=, <, >, &&, ||
- Unary operators: !, - (negation)
- Parenthesized expressions: (expr)

Generators must be recursive with a max-depth parameter (start with depth 3-4). Use rapid's Deferred for recursive references. Ensure brackets are balanced by construction. Include array literal generator: [expr, ...] with 0-5 elements.

Include unit tests verifying generated expressions are syntactically valid at various depths.

title: Build test context/payload generator
description:
Create internal/testing/exprgen/context.go with rapid generators for test contexts:

- SampleContext() generates a payload with a mix of:
  - Flat objects with string/number/boolean/null fields
  - Nested objects (1-2 levels)
  - Arrays of objects, arrays of primitives
  - Empty objects and arrays
- Variable reference generator (IdentGen) that only produces identifiers in scope: payload, payload.field for fields that exist in the generated context

The context generator must produce both the Go value (for passing to the runner) and the JSON string (for use as CLI input). Include unit tests.

title: Build core expression generator with script wrapping
description:
Create internal/testing/exprgen/generator.go that composes the literal, operator, and context generators into a complete expression generator.

- Expression(maxDepth) returns a rapid generator that produces full infomunge source-level expression strings
- WrapScript(expr) wraps an expression in a valid script with header: '%im 0.1\noutput application/json\n---\nexpr'
- Feature subset parameter to control which expression forms are enabled (start with arithmetic/comparison/arrays only)
- Lightweight validity guard: skip generated cases that fail preprocessing with a syntax error (don't count toward test budget)

Include generator_test.go with self-tests:
- Generated expressions have bounded depth
- Generated expressions are syntactically valid (pass through preprocessor without panic)
- Feature subset parameter actually restricts output

title: Implement no-panic property test
description:
Create internal/testing/properties/nopanic_test.go with the foundational property test:

- For any generated expression and context, evaluating the expression should either produce a result or return an error — never panic
- Use rapid.Check with a high iteration count (e.g., 10000)
- Recover from panics and report them as test failures with the expression and context that caused the panic
- Include the determinism property: eval(expr, ctx) called twice produces identical output
- Include the type consistency property: typeOf(eval(expr)) returns a valid type string

This single test file is the highest-value deliverable — it will likely surface bugs immediately.

title: Implement failure artifact capture
description:
Create internal/testing/failures/artifact.go:

- Artifact struct recording: minimized expression, input/payload, violated property name, actual vs expected result (or panic stack trace), original pre-shrink expression, random seed for reproducibility
- SaveArtifact() writes a JSON file to tmp/intensive-testing/failures/ with a sequential ID and timestamp in the filename (e.g., 001_nopanic_2026-02-10T14:30:00.json)
- Deduplication via fingerprinting: hash of (minimized expression + violated property). Skip saving if fingerprint already exists in the failures directory
- LoadArtifacts() reads all artifacts from the directory for reporting

Include unit tests for serialization round-trip and deduplication logic. Ensure tmp/intensive-testing/failures/ is in .gitignore.

title: Implement cucumber scenario auto-generator
description:
Create internal/testing/failures/scenario_gen.go:

- GenerateScenario(artifact) produces a .feature scenario skeleton from a failure artifact
- Template includes: comment with property name, shrunk expression, original seed; Given step with input payload; When step with script; Then step with placeholder for expected result or error
- WriteCandidateScenario() saves the generated .feature text to tmp/intensive-testing/candidates/ for human review
- Batch mode: GenerateAllCandidates() processes all artifacts that don't already have a corresponding candidate

Example output:
  # Auto-generated from intensive testing failure 001
  # Property: no-panic
  Scenario: Expression does not panic on null index arithmetic
    Given input payload is ...
    When infomunge processes ...
    Then the error should contain '...'

Include unit tests verifying generated scenarios are valid Gherkin syntax. Ensure tmp/intensive-testing/candidates/ is in .gitignore.

title: Add object literal and dot/index access generators
description:
Expand the expression generator to support:

- Object literals: {key: expr, ...} with 0-5 fields, string keys
- Dot access: expr.field (field names drawn from context shape)
- Index access: expr[expr] (integer and string indices)
- Range index: expr[expr to expr]

Update the ExprGen OneOf to include these forms. Ensure generated field names are valid identifiers. Add generator self-tests for syntactic validity of new forms.

The RewriteWithDepth function in preprocessor.go is complex (130+ lines) with nested conditionals. The handleIfElse, handleAndOr, handleNewline, handleOpenBrace, handleCloseBrace, and handleUnquotedKey methods help but the main loop is still hard to follow.
